title: Designing a Production-Grade AWS Architecture: Breaking Down a Real Interview Question
content: 9 min readJan 31, 2026--Hey all, it is always great writing to you.This one took a bit more effort to put together because I had to turn a slightly sloppy situation into something I could actually learn from.DevOps, DevSecOps, and Cloud interviews are evolving. These days, you rarely get asked questions like “What is a Terraform state file?” or “List the components of a Kubernetes cluster.” Either the interview process has changed, or I’m getting more senior in my role … probably a bit of both. What I do see a lot more now are whiteboard-style interviews and architecture questions.And that makes sense. Architecture sits at the intersection of code, infrastructure, and system design — an area of the SDLC where understanding is hard to fake. You can generate quick answers with AI now, but reasoning through architecture, trade-offs, and tooling in real time still requires experience and clear thinking.I prepared fairly well for this interview, fairly, because if I had prepared perfectly, I probably wouldn’t be writing this article. I also performed well overall, but someone else performed better. Life happens.Instead of crying over spilled milk, I like to document my experiences. I go back to interviews, review what I said, revisit the questions I struggled with, and dig into the topics that felt shaky. Sometimes that means reading more, sometimes it means building things hands-on , but the goal is simple: don’t fail the same way twice.In this interview, I was comfortable with most areas: security, security scanner configuration, Infrastructure as Code with Terraform, Linux administration, secrets management, documentation, and CI/CD. Where I could have done better was architecture.So in this article, I’ve written out the architecture question I was asked and walked through a more refined and structured version of my answer, explaining the logic, the tooling, and the diagram in a way that’s clearer, more defensible, and more interview-friendly.I hope it helps.Architecture QuestionContextYou are designing a production-grade cloud architecture on AWS for a company operating in a fintech-like environment, where availability, security, and scalability matter.The company uses an AWS Organization with multiple accounts. One of these accounts is designated as the production account.Core RequirementsInside the production AWS account, you are required to deploy two microservices with the following characteristics:1. PlatformThe services must run on Amazon EKS (Elastic Kubernetes Service).Kubernetes is the primary compute and orchestration layer.2. ServicesService A: A public REST API, Must be accessible from the internetService B: A private REST API, Must NOT be publicly accessible. Can only be reached internally, specifically by Service A3. Data LayerEach service has its own database.Databases are PostgreSQL.Databases must be isolated appropriately and treated as production data stores4. NetworkingYou are free to design the VPC layoutYou must decide: Number of VPCs. Subnet structure (public vs private). How traffic flows from users to the services. How services communicate with each other. Direct internet access to private components must be controlled5. Production ConstraintsThe setup must include:High availability: Tolerance for failures, Use of multiple Availability ZonesFault tolerance: No single point of failure, A design that could later support autoscaling. (You do not need to implement autoscaling yet, but the design must not prevent it)6. Out of Scope (Explicitly)For this exercise:CI/CD pipelines are not requiredApplication-level code is not requiredYou are focused on infrastructure and architecture onlyMy Refined Architecture AnswerThe LogicI’d be explaining the logic and tooling first before drawing an architectural diagram because, it is important to clarify the reasoning and constraints that drive the design. Diagrams are a visual representation of considerations already made, and drawing boxes first without a clear mental model often leads to incorrect or misleading designs.The requirements of this system immediately establish a few non-negotiable principles.First, this is a production environment. That implies high availability, fault tolerance, and secure defaults. Any design that places critical components in a single Availability Zone, exposes internal services publicly, or tightly couples services together would already be failing basic production expectations.Second, the system consists of two services with different exposure levels. One service is intentionally public and must be reachable from the internet. The other is intentionally private and must never be directly exposed. This single requirement alone dictates the need for network segmentation, controlled ingress, and explicit service-to-service communication paths. Public and private workloads cannot be treated uniformly, and this is one factor I emphasised on during my interview.Third, the compute platform is Kubernetes on Amazon EKS. This introduces a clear separation of concerns:AWS is responsible for the underlying infrastructure, networking, and managed control plane.Kubernetes is responsible for workload orchestration, service discovery, and pod-level networking.A correct design must respect both layers and avoid mixing responsibilities between them.Fourth, each service owns its own PostgreSQL database. This reinforces service isolation and eliminates shared state. From an architectural standpoint, this means databases should be private, unreachable from the internet, and accessible only by the service that owns them. It also implies that database availability and security must be considered independently of application availability.Finally, scalability and growth are implied even if not explicitly required. The architecture must allow for:Horizontal scaling of servicesIndependent scaling of each microserviceFuture additions such as autoscaling, observability, or service mesh adoptionA rigid or overly simplified design would block these paths.Given these constraints, the logical approach is:Use a single production VPC with clearly separated public and private subnets across multiple Availability Zones.2. Place all EKS worker nodes in private subnets, ensuring no direct internet exposure of pods.3. Expose the public service through a controlled ingress mechanism, rather than directly exposing Kubernetes nodes.4. Keep the private service accessible only via internal networking within the cluster.5. Place PostgreSQL databases in private subnets, with tightly scoped access rules.6. Let AWS networking primitives handle ingress and isolation, while Kubernetes handles service-level communication.Only after these decisions are clearly understood does it make sense to draw an architectural diagram. The diagram then becomes a tool for communication, not a guessing exercise. In an interview, you want to explain your logic aloud for your interviewer so that even if you are not so much a great architect or you do not get enough time to draw, you have gotten your point of reasoning along.The next thing now, is to translate the logic into a diagram.Translating the Logic into Architecture DiagramPress enter or click to view image in full sizeArchitectural Diagram of the flow of trafficPress enter or click to view image in full sizeArchitectural Diagram showing the flow of traffic in the Private SubnetsArchitecture Walkthrough: Components and Traffic Flow1. Entry Point, Application Load Balancer (ALB): The traffic into the system begins at the Application Load Balancer (ALB).The ALB is deployed in the public subnets of the production VPC and is associated with an Internet Gateway, which allows it to receive traffic from the internet. End users access the system over HTTPS (port 443), and all external traffic terminates at the ALB. The ALB is the only internet-facing component in the architecture. No application workloads or databases are exposed directly to the internet.From the ALB, traffic is forwarded to the Kubernetes cluster through a Kubernetes Ingress.2. Public Subnets, What Lives There and Why:The public subnets exist solely to host infrastructure components that must be reachable from the internet.They contain:The Application Load BalancerA route to the Internet GatewayThey do not contain:Application pods for the services or Kubernetes worker nodesDatabasesThis separation ensures that only controlled ingress points are publicly reachable, significantly reducing the attack surface of the system.3. Ingress, Bridging AWS and Kubernetes:The ALB does not send traffic directly to application pods.Instead, it forwards traffic to a target group managed by the AWS Load Balancer Controller, which integrates the ALB with Kubernetes. The controller translates Kubernetes Ingress resources into ALB listener rules and target groups.Traffic flows as follows:ALB receives HTTPS trafficALB forwards traffic to targets in the private subnetsKubernetes Ingress routes the request to the appropriate serviceThis is the critical bridge between AWS networking and Kubernetes service routing.4. Private Subnets, Application and Data Isolation:The private subnets host all sensitive and internal components.They contain:EKS worker nodesKubernetes pods for both servicesPostgreSQL databases for each serviceThese subnets have no direct route to the internet, meaning resources within them cannot be accessed externally unless traffic is explicitly forwarded through the ALB.5. Amazon EKS Cluster, Compute and Orchestration:The Amazon EKS cluster runs on worker nodes deployed across multiple private subnets and Availability Zones. This ensures:High availabilityFault toleranceEven distribution of workloadsBoth services run as Kubernetes workloads on the same cluster but remain logically isolated through Kubernetes primitives.6. Service A, Public API:Service A is a public-facing REST API.Although it is publicly accessible, it still runs entirely inside the private subnets. It becomes “public” only because:It is exposed via a Kubernetes IngressThe Ingress is backed by the ALBTraffic flow to Service A:User sends HTTPS requestALB receives the requestIngress routes the request to Service AKubernetes forwards traffic to the appropriate podAt no point does Service A require a public IP or a public subnet.7. Service B, Private API:Service B is a private internal REST API.It is exposed only as a ClusterIP service, meaning it is:Not reachable from the internetNot reachable through the ALBAccessible only from within the Kubernetes clusterService B is designed to be consumed exclusively by Service A.Traffic flow to Service B:Service A sends an internal request using Kubernetes service discoveryTraffic stays entirely within the private subnetsNo external hops are involved8. Service-to-Service CommunicationCommunication between Service A and Service B uses internal Kubernetes networking.This provides:Low latencyNo public exposureClear trust boundariesBecause both services run in the same EKS cluster, Kubernetes DNS resolves Service B internally, and traffic never leaves the cluster.9. Databases, Per-Service Ownership:Each service owns its own PostgreSQL database, deployed in private subnets.Service A connects only to Database AService B connects only to Database BThere is no shared databaseThis enforces:Strong service isolationIndependent scalingReduced blast radiusDatabases are not accessible from the internet and accept connections only from their respective services.10. Security Controls (Implicit but Critical)Security is enforced through multiple layers:Subnet isolation prevents direct internet accessSecurity groups restrict which components can communicateIngress rules explicitly control public exposureThe result is a system where:Public access is intentional and limitedInternal components remain private by defaultTraffic paths are explicit and auditableClosing off….Basically, architecture is not about drawing boxes or memorising cloud services. It is about understanding boundaries, responsibilities, and flow and being able to explain why each component exists.This exercise reinforced an important lesson for me: public and private are exposure decisions, not exactly placement decisions. Both services run in private subnets, yet one is intentionally exposed through a controlled ingress while the other remains internal by design. The difference lies in how traffic is routed and constrained, not where the workloads physically sit.By starting from requirements, clarifying trust boundaries, and reasoning through networking and service interactions before drawing a diagram, the resulting architecture becomes easier to explain, easier to secure, and easier to evolve. The diagram then becomes a communication tool, not a source of confusion.Whether this design originated from an interview question or a real production system is ultimately irrelevant. I just like to think that the value comes from the process of breaking down a problem, making deliberate trade-offs, and arriving at a solution that is both logical and defensible.That process, more than the diagram itself, is what good architecture is built on, and I absolutely enjoyed every bit of this.Thank you for reading and…Kindly clap and follow me for more updates and articles. Thank you again, dear reader!The Cloud Fairy 🌩️🧚‍♀️👩‍💻
